output.text_response:
**Mode:** Create — no prior plans existed for q_001.
**Question:** "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?" (q_001)

**Facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn birth: ~1845, Ireland (source: 1850 census, dwelling 84)
- Patrick Flynn death: 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (source: death cert no. 4521, S3)
- Thomas Flynn birth: ~1818, Ireland (in tree, no source attached)
- Relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick): cited in S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census, dwelling 112), S3 (death cert) — but only the 1850 census has assertions extracted for q_001
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills) is in the tree sources but not attached to any facts or assertions
- The proof summary (ps_001) is at tier "possible" resting solely on 1850 census co-enumeration

---

**Plan pl_002 — items in execution order:**

- **pli_004** — vital_record, Schuylkill County, PA, 1908, FamilySearch. Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3, cert no. 4521) is already in the tree for his death fact but no parentage assertions have been extracted. A PA 1908 death cert typically names both parents including the mother's maiden name — highest-probability direct source.
- **pli_005** — census, Schuylkill County, PA, 1860, FamilySearch. S2 (1860 census, dwelling 112) is cited in the tree's R1 relationship but no q_001 assertions have been drawn from it. Extends co-enumeration evidence one decade; may reveal siblings or wife who identify the mother. Free, name-searchable.
- **pli_006** — census, Schuylkill County, PA, 1870, Ancestry (collection 7163, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/). Specifically included per delegation. Patrick ~25, Thomas ~52. Adds a third decade of co-enumeration evidence; the 1870 census names all household members by name, age, and birthplace. Paid, name-searchable.
- **pli_007** — census, Schuylkill County, PA, 1880, FamilySearch. The first census to name each person's explicit relationship to the head; if Patrick (~35) appears in Thomas's household the relationship field elevates this beyond inference. Also names parents' birthplaces. Free, name-searchable.
- **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County, PA, 1900, FamilySearch. Patrick ~55, likely still in Schuylkill County (died there 1908). The 1900 schedule asks parents' birthplaces by country, corroborating Irish origins for both parents. Free, name-searchable.
- **pli_009** — probate, Schuylkill County, PA, 1855–1900, FamilySearch. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) could have died ages 37–82; S4 (Register of Wills) is in the tree but no probate facts have been recorded. A will naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence. Browse-only; image group 007936749 (1851–1930) covers the range.
- **pli_010** — church, Schuylkill County, PA, 1835–1860, FamilySearch. Search for Thomas Flynn and Patrick's mother's marriage — required for a parentage question. Supplies the mother's maiden name and confirms the couple before Patrick's ~1845 birth. Note: marriage may have been in Ireland before emigration; Pennsylvania church records searched first as accessible.
- **pli_011** — church, Schuylkill County, PA, 1842–1895, FamilySearch. Browse-only fallback for pli_010. Image group 007936751 may include marriage registers, sibling baptisms, or burial entries not yet indexed. *fallback_for: pli_010.*
- **pli_012** — vital_record, Schuylkill County, PA, 1870–1908, FamilySearch. Patrick's own marriage record; may name parents or provide age/birthplace corroborating the parentage inference. Schuylkill County marriage records image group 007936753 (1870–1910) is browse-only.
- **pli_013** — immigration, Schuylkill County, PA, 1849–1880, FamilySearch. Thomas's naturalization petition commonly names country and parish of origin, arrival date, and in later forms wife and children — could place Patrick as Thomas's son and name the mother. Image group 007936750 (1849–1915) is browse-only.

**Fallback:** pli_011 (church records image browse) is the fallback for pli_010 (church records name search).

**Total:** 10 searches across 4 census years, death certificate, probate, church records (2 items), county marriage records, and naturalization records.

---

The plan starts with the record most likely to answer directly: Patrick's 1908 death certificate, which Pennsylvania law required to name both parents. It then works through census records already partially in the project (1860), the specifically requested 1870 Ancestry census, and the 1880 and 1900 FamilySearch censuses. The 1880 census is particularly important as the first to state each person's relationship to the household head. After censuses: Thomas Flynn's probate records, the marriage record of Thomas and Patrick's mother (needed for the mother's maiden name), a browse-only fallback for those church records, Patrick's own marriage record, and Thomas's naturalization papers as the FAN-cluster item.

FamilySearch items are sequenced before the paid Ancestry item. Browse-only image groups are sequenced after name-searchable collections.

**Next step:** Search FamilySearch records (death certificate, 1860, 1880, 1900 censuses, probate, church, county marriage, naturalization) and separately run the 1870 census search on Ancestry.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

If Patrick (approximately 35) appears in Thomas's household or Thomas appears in Patrick's, the explicit relationship field — rather than inferred co-enumeration — would substantially strengthen the parentage case. The 1880 census also names parents' birthplaces. Name-searchable on FamilySearch; free. Search Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

The 1900 US Federal Census asks each person to report both parents' birthplaces by country. Patrick (approximately 55) likely remained in Schuylkill County through 1900 given he died there in 1908. His entry would corroborate Irish origins for both parents, and if Thomas or other family members appear, their entries extend the evidence chain. The 1900 census also records the number of years married, which supports or refines estimates for Patrick's own marriage. Name-searchable on FamilySearch; free.

Thomas Flynn (born approximately 1818) died at an unknown date; S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills) is already in the tree as a source but no probate facts or assertions have been recorded from it. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence; an estate inventory or sale record naming him as an heir is indirect but corroborating. Date window based on Thomas's lifespan: he could have died between roughly 1855 and 1900 (ages approximately 37 to 82). The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851-1930) covers the same range. Browse both. The loc_001 locality entry confirms probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and Patrick's mother — required for a parentage question. The marriage record would supply the mother's maiden name (which censuses and death records routinely omit) and confirm the couple as a unit before Patrick's birth approximately 1845. Note: because Patrick's birth fact in the tree records Ireland as his birthplace, the couple may have married in Ireland before emigrating; Pennsylvania church records are searched first as the accessible option, with the date range extended to 1860 to allow for a possible second marriage or a delayed registration. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Per loc_001, Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875). Search Thomas Flynn and variant spellings Flyn, Flinn.

Browse-only fallback for the name-searchable church records search in pli_007. Image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895) covers the target period and may include marriage registers, baptismal entries for Patrick's siblings, or burial entries not yet indexed in the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection. Per loc_001, some church and naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. Browse page-by-page if the name search in pli_007 yields nothing.

Patrick's own marriage record, if one exists, may state his age and birthplace or, in later county forms, his parents' names. The Schuylkill County marriage records image group 007936752 covers 1870-1910 and is browse-only (personCount 0). Patrick disappears from the tree after his 1908 death with no spouse listed; this item tests whether he married and what that record contains about his origins. A marriage bondsman or surety (frequently the bride's father or a close male relative of the groom) also constitutes FAN-cluster evidence that may identify a sibling or associate of Patrick who can corroborate parentage.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization record is the required FAN-cluster item for this parentage question. As a male Irish immigrant who appears in the 1850 Schuylkill County census, Thomas almost certainly petitioned for citizenship in the county. A naturalization petition commonly names the applicant's country and sometimes province or parish of origin, his arrival date, and in later forms (post-1906 Declaration of Intention) his wife's name and the names and ages of his children — evidence that could place Patrick as Thomas's son and name the mother. The Schuylkill County naturalization records image group 007936750 (1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). Thomas's lifespan (born approximately 1818) sets the window's upper bound at approximately 1880.

**Mode: Create** — first plan for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845 in **Ireland** (sourced to S1, 1850 census, dwelling 84); death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (sourced to S3, death cert no. 4521)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth ~1818, Ireland; no source attached to that fact; no death date in tree
- Relationship R1 (Thomas parent of Patrick): sourced at quality 2 to S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census, dwelling 112), and S3 (death cert) — all three are tree source descriptions, but only two assertions from S1 (a_004, a_005) have been formally extracted for q_001
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is a tree source description with no assertions extracted for q_001
- **Patrick's mother is entirely absent from the tree** — she has never been identified
- Proof summary ps_001 is at tier "possible," shortfall "gap"; post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records explicitly flagged as not yet searched

**Plan pl_002 — 9 items in execution order:**

- **pli_004** — vital_record, Pennsylvania (statewide), 1908, FamilySearch: Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3, no. 4521) is already a tree source description linked to R1 but not formally extracted for q_001; the informant's statement names father and mother — single highest-yield remaining source for the mother's identity; try Flynn/Flyn variants
- **pli_005** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch (collection 1417683, name-searchable): first federal census to state each person's relationship to the head; a "wife" entry in Thomas's household names the mother; a "son" label for Patrick is direct parentage evidence
- **pli_006** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1860, FamilySearch (collection 1473181, name-searchable): S2 is a tree source linked to R1 but no assertions extracted; household order in 1860 may reveal a woman between Thomas and Patrick as his mother; try Flynn/Flyn variants
- **pli_007** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch (collection 1325221, name-searchable): Patrick (~55) is alive; 1900 schedule records parents' nativity; if enumerated with Thomas (~82), co-residence continues; parents' birthplace fields add geographic context
- **pli_008** — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1840-1870, FamilySearch (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable): dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, required for any parentage question; names the wife's maiden surname; if no PA record is found, Irish Catholic records are the next step
- **pli_009** — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1920, FamilySearch (collection 1999196, browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749, browse-only (personCount 0)): date range set by Thomas's plausible lifespan (born ~1818); S4 is a tree source description with no q_001 assertions; a will naming "my son Patrick" is direct parentage evidence and may name the wife; image-by-image browse required
- **pli_010** — immigration, Schuylkill County PA, 1849-1915, FamilySearch (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0)): FAN-directed search; Thomas's naturalization declaration may list wife and minor children — the mother's name and Patrick's confirmation as son; browse-only, image-by-image required
- **pli_011** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch (collection 1438024, name-searchable): fills 1860-1880 gap; no relationship labels but household order may show a woman with Thomas and Patrick; lower priority than 1860 and 1880
- **pli_012** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/): paid fallback for pli_011; same underlying record set, duplicate-access only

**Subject's own death entry (baptism not in PA — born in Ireland ~1845):** pli_004

**Total scope: 9 searches** — 8 on FamilySearch (7 requiring the search-records skill; 3 are browse-only image groups), 1 on Ancestry (search-external-sites). Fallback relationship: pli_012 follows pli_011 if the FamilySearch 1870 census yields nothing.

The plan starts with the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate, which was already noted in the family tree but never formally searched, because it directly asks for the deceased's parents by name. It then works through the federal censuses for 1880, 1860, and 1900 (in that order of usefulness for naming family relationships), followed by a dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage record in the local Catholic registers — the one record most likely to supply the mother's maiden name. Thomas's own probate file and his naturalization papers round out the search, since both types of documents often listed a man's wife and children. A search of the 1870 census closes out the plan as a lower-priority gap-filler, with Ancestry as a paid fallback if the FamilySearch version turns up nothing.

The next step is to execute the FamilySearch items starting with the 1908 death certificate search, followed by the census and church record searches — all through the search-records skill. The Ancestry 1870 item waits unless the FamilySearch search for that year is unsuccessful.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The Seeger household entry would list both parents by name and all their children with birth dates, making it the most comprehensive single source for the full family unit. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

If Thomas Flynn was alive in Schuylkill County in 1880, any child listed in his household would be documented as 'son' or 'daughter' — the first explicit indirect evidence of the sibling relationship, which strengthens the inference that Thomas was Patrick's father. Sibling names identified in the 1850 and 1860 censuses (already in hand) guide this search. Also search for Patrick Flynn's own 1880 household to identify siblings co-residing or named; Patrick would be approximately 35 and likely had his own household. Variant spellings to try: Flinn, Flyn.

The United States Census, 1870 collection is name-searchable. The 1870 census does not record explicit relationships (that column did not appear until 1880), but finding Thomas Flynn's household at this date identifies any children still with him between the already-searched 1860 and the planned 1880 searches. Any sibling of Patrick present in this household is a FAN record corroborating that Thomas headed the Flynn family unit across multiple decades. Sibling names identified here become leads for their own death certificates (pli_011). Variant spellings: Flinn, Flyn.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 in Ireland, so his own baptism is an Irish record, not a Pennsylvania one. Any siblings born after the family's arrival (circa 1845-1850 onward) would have been baptized in a Schuylkill County parish; a sibling's baptism entry names both parents — Thomas Flynn and Patrick's unnamed mother — and is direct evidence of the family unit. Irish Catholic emigrants in the anthracite coal region predominantly joined Roman Catholic parishes under the Diocese of Philadelphia; the collection covers both Catholic and Protestant denominations. The browse-only church volume (image group 007936751, 1842-1895) is a fallback if the indexed search underperforms. Also search for Thomas Flynn as a baptismal sponsor or witness, which would place him in the parish community.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. This item targets Thomas Flynn's marriage in Pennsylvania specifically. Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland, so Thomas's first marriage likely occurred in Ireland before emigration; however, if Thomas remarried or if the first marriage was performed upon arrival, a church marriage register in Schuylkill County would name both spouses. A marriage entry: (a) confirms the couple as a documented unit; (b) supplies Patrick's mother's maiden name, which neither the 1850 nor the 1860 census records; (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth, corroborates Thomas as the father named in only indirect and secondary sources. Note: this marriage record alone does not establish that Patrick is their child — a household or baptism record placing Patrick with this couple remains necessary. Also search for burial entries for Thomas Flynn's wife (mother unknown), which may give her name.

Pennsylvania statewide civil death registration began in 1906 (as noted in the locality guide for Schuylkill County). Any sibling of Patrick Flynn who survived to 1906 would have a state death certificate. The informant on a sibling's death certificate — typically that sibling's own child — would be a grandchild of Thomas Flynn and a closer informant than Patrick's son-in-law James Brown (the secondary informant on Patrick's 1908 certificate). A sibling's death certificate naming Thomas Flynn as father is a second independent, FAN-sourced statement of parentage converging with the death certificate already in hand. Sibling given names come from the 1850 and 1860 census households of Thomas Flynn. Variant spellings for index searches: Flinn, Flyn.

The Schuylkill County marriage records volume (image group 007936753, 1870-1910) is browse-only (personCount 0); the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable and covers church marriages in the same period. Pennsylvania did not require statewide marriage registration until 1906; pre-1906 marriages are in county bonds and licenses or church registers. A marriage bond or license for Patrick Flynn could name Thomas Flynn as a consenting surety or parent — placing Thomas in an official document in relation to Patrick. The church marriage register might likewise name Patrick's father. Patrick was born ~1845 and would have been of marriageable age from approximately 1865 onward.

The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records volume (image group 007936750, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). Irish immigrants who naturalized typically filed a declaration of intent 2-7 years after arrival; Thomas Flynn arriving circa 1845-1849 might have declared intent in 1851-1856. A declaration of intent or certificate of naturalization names the declarant's country and sometimes county of origin, and in some periods names the spouse and minor children — directly linking Thomas to the family in an official court document. Even where children are not named, the record confirms the county of residence and may identify the exact parish of origin in Ireland, opening the way to Irish records that could document the family before emigration.

The delegation did not include authorization to execute; awaiting your direction.

The project is trying to prove that Patrick Flynn (born around 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) was the son of Thomas Flynn. The two census records and a death certificate found so far only show Patrick living in Thomas's household and a son-in-law's statement naming Thomas — strong circumstantial evidence, but not enough for a definitive conclusion. This new plan shifts the strategy to records of Thomas's family and associates rather than records of Patrick alone. It will first look for Thomas Flynn's will or estate file (which could name Patrick directly as an heir), then search the 1880 and 1870 censuses for other children of Thomas still in his household (the 1880 census being the first to state each person's relationship to the head), followed by church records for the baptisms of siblings born in Pennsylvania after the family arrived, Thomas's own marriage record, death certificates of any of Patrick's siblings who survived past 1906, Patrick's own marriage record (which may name his father as a consenting party), and finally Thomas's naturalization papers (which sometimes name a wife and children).

The next step is to run these searches on FamilySearch, starting with the probate browse and the 1880 census name-search.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

These columns would show whether Michael was Irish-born or Pennsylvania-born, directly bearing on whether the move was an internal relocation or an immigrant settling near chain-migrated kin. Use surname variants Sheahan / Sheehan.

If Patrick was employed in the anthracite mines and had an established household when Michael arrived, that family connection is a candidate explanation for Michael's migration that the plan must test alongside the family-tradition claim that mining work alone was the draw.

- Brother Patrick (I2): Schuylkill County 1875, with a deed purchase from James Kelly seven years before Michael arrived

---

**The 8 plan items:**

| # | Type | Target | Purpose |
|---|------|--------|---------|
| pli_001 | Census 1880 | FamilySearch | Michael's exact location and occupation just before the move |
| pli_002 | Census 1870 | FamilySearch | Where was Michael 12 years before? Was he already mining? |
| pli_003 | Census 1880 (FAN) | FamilySearch | Brother Patrick's 1880 household — tests chain-migration hypothesis |
| pli_004 | Naturalization 1849–1915 | Schuylkill County, browse-only | Michael's country of origin, port of entry, prior US residence |
| pli_005 | Church records 1842–1895 | Schuylkill County | Catholic parish anchors him to a specific mining town post-1882 |
| pli_006 | Census 1900 | FamilySearch | Confirms sustained settlement; captures immigration year |
| pli_007 | Land / Deed records 1880–1900 | Schuylkill County | Did Michael buy land near Patrick? Economic independence vs. company housing |
| pli_008 | Census 1860 | FamilySearch | Whole Sheahan family before 1870 — did they immigrate together? |

---

**Core strategy:** The central question is whether Michael moved for *work* (already a miner, moved within the industry), *family* (following brother Patrick who had settled there in 1875), or both. openQuestions.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US Federal Census (FamilySearch collection 1417683, name-searchable) falls two years before Michael's documented 1882 arrival in Schuylkill County. Finding Michael will show his exact Pennsylvania location, occupation, and household in 1880 — the single most important record for establishing where he was immediately before the move and what economic circumstances preceded it. If he was already in a coal county (Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland), it would show an industry-driven move within the anthracite field rather than a first entry into mining. Search variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan alongside Sheahan.

The tree records a 1870 Pennsylvania residence for Michael (fact F1, source S1, derivative, quality 1) but gives no specific place within the state. The 1870 US Federal Census (FamilySearch collection 1438024, name-searchable) would confirm his specific location, his occupation (miner or not), household members, and state of birth — establishing whether he had a coal-mining background a full decade before the 1882 Schuylkill County move. Search variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan alongside Sheahan.

FAN item targeting Patrick Sheahan (I2, brother). Patrick purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (source S2, Deed Book 42, p. 118, from James Kelly), seven years before Michael's 1882 arrival. Locating Patrick in the 1880 US Federal Census (FamilySearch collection 1417683, name-searchable) would show his occupation, neighborhood, and household composition, and whether other Sheahan family members were already settled there. This tests the chain-migration hypothesis — that Michael followed an established family network — against the family-tradition claim that work alone drove the move. Search variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan.

Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849-1915 (FamilySearch volume 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0)). If Michael was born in Ireland, his declaration of intention or naturalization petition would state his country of origin, port of entry, date of arrival in the United States, and sometimes his prior US residence. These details bear directly on whether the 1882 move was part of a transatlantic chain-migration pattern — Irish immigrant to established Pennsylvania coal community — or a secondary migration within the US. Browse image by image; search index for Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan.

Two sources cover Catholic and other parish registers: the indexed Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (FamilySearch SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, 1708-1985) and the browse-only image group 007936751 (1842-1895). The locality guide (loc_001) notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia, serving Irish immigrant mining communities. A baptism of a child, a marriage, or a burial placed in a specific mining town after 1882 would anchor Michael to a particular parish community, helping distinguish work-driven relocation from family- or parish-network-driven settlement. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH first (name-searchable); browse volume 007936751 if no match. Variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan.

The 1900 US Federal Census (FamilySearch collection 1325221, name-searchable) recorded immigration year and length of US residence for foreign-born persons, along with nativity, occupation, and naturalization status. Finding Michael in Schuylkill County in 1900 would confirm sustained settlement 18 years after the move, show his immigration year (testing Irish origin), reveal whether he naturalized, and confirm whether coal mining remained his occupation — all directly relevant to whether the 1882 move was economically motivated and permanent. Note: the 1890 census was destroyed in an 1921 fire and cannot fill the 1880-1900 gap. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan.

Schuylkill County Deed Records, 1815-1900 (FamilySearch volume 007936752, 22% record-searchable). The locality guide (loc_001) notes that coal-region laborers in this county typically leased rather than purchased land from mining companies, so a deed in Michael's name would suggest a more permanent, independent economic footing. Patrick's 1875 purchase is already documented in the tree (S2, Deed Book 42, p. 118). Searching volume 007936752 for Michael from 1882 onward would reveal whether he settled near his brother or in a different township, speaking to whether family proximity or workplace access governed his choice of community. The 22% searchable figure means most of the volume must be browsed image by image.

The 1860 US Federal Census (FamilySearch collection 1473181, name-searchable) would show the Sheahan household when Michael was a child or young adult — before the 1870 Pennsylvania residence the tree records. Finding the family in 1860 would establish the parent(s) named as I3, their state or country of birth, and the region where Michael grew up, answering whether the family immigrated from Ireland together or Michael came later on his own. This contextual record helps distinguish whether the Pennsylvania-to-Schuylkill move was a family or individual decision. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan with parents and Patrick together.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: All three tree facts for Michael Sheahan — 1870 Pennsylvania residence, 1882 Schuylkill County residence, and 1882 Miner occupation — are unsourced assumptions. The 1880 US Federal Census (name-searchable) is the record closest to 1882 and the highest-probability anchor: it will either confirm he was already in Schuylkill County as a miner by June 1880 (moving the arrival date earlier) or place him in a different county or state, establishing the origin of the migration. Also look for other Sheahan or Sheehan households in the same Schuylkill County enumeration district — co-residing or neighboring family members would support a chain-migration reading. Try surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan. Collection: United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683).

The tree records an unsourced 1870 residence in Pennsylvania without naming the county. The 1870 US Federal Census (name-searchable) would identify the specific county and occupation that year, anchoring the migration's origin point. If the 1870 entry shows him outside Schuylkill County and the 1880 entry places him in Schuylkill, the move occurred between those two dates rather than a single jump to 1882. Try surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan. Collection: United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024).

The 1900 US Federal Census (name-searchable) confirms continued Schuylkill County residence roughly 18 years after the tradition-date arrival and typically records occupation, birthplace, and — critically for an Irish immigrant — the year of immigration and years naturalized. These immigration fields directly address whether Sheahan came from Ireland and when, which underpins any chain-migration or economic-pull explanation for the move. Try surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan. Collection: United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221).

The Irish surname Sheahan strongly suggests Roman Catholic affiliation. The loc_001 locality entry confirms that Schuylkill County Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout this period and that civil registration did not begin until 1906 — making church records the primary pre-1906 source. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable and covers 1708–1985. A baptism, marriage, or death entry for Michael Sheahan or a family member in a Schuylkill County parish would show when he first appears in local parish rolls, corroborating the circa-1882 arrival. A transfer letter or marriage-record declaration of a prior parish would also speak to pre-Schuylkill residence. Try variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan.

Schuylkill County naturalization records 1849–1915 survive as a browse-only image group (personCount 0). The loc_001 locality entry explicitly flags that some naturalization films for the anthracite region are browse-only, consistent with this result. If Sheahan was Irish-born, his declaration of intent — typically filed shortly after arriving in the county — could record country and sometimes town of birth, the date of US arrival, and prior US residence. Filing in Schuylkill County itself corroborates settlement there. Browse image group 007936750 image by image, checking entries under Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan.

The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines published annual reports for each anthracite coal district from the 1870s onward. These reports list operating collieries by name, the operator, and fatal or serious accidents — sometimes naming individual miners. Locating Michael Sheahan in a report tied to a named Schuylkill County colliery would be direct evidence that his residence there was tied to coal-mining employment, not merely coincident with it. These records are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, Harrisburg) and are not indexed online; a written or in-person inquiry is needed. This is the primary occupation-specific record for the question.

Fallback if the 1870 US Federal Census does not locate Michael Sheahan in Pennsylvania. The 1860 census (name-searchable) extends the search window earlier; if he immigrated from Ireland in the late 1850s, this may be the first US census in which he appears. Consistent household members between 1860 and a later census entry also help confirm identity when the name is common. Try surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan. Collection: United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181).

Fallback if the 1900 US Federal Census does not locate Michael Sheahan in Schuylkill County. Indexing gaps exist for common Irish surnames in the 1900 schedules. The 1910 census (name-searchable) still records birthplace, occupation, and years of immigration. Even a 1910 entry listing him as a retired or aging miner in Schuylkill County supports a decades-long coal-mining residence. Try surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan. Collection: United States Census, 1910 (collection 1488411).

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

- Patrick Flynn (I1): Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (source S3, Death cert. no. 4521)

| # | Type | Place | Years | Repository | Rationale |
|---|------|-------|-------|------------|-----------|

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, Death cert. no. 4521) is already in the project tree and cited in R1 (ParentChild relationship Thomas→Patrick, quality 2), but no parentage assertions have been extracted from it for q_001. Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906, so this 1908 certificate exists and typically includes dedicated fields for the decedent's father's name and mother's maiden name. If the informant knew Patrick's parents, this record provides direct derivative evidence of both parents simultaneously — making it the highest-priority item. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried if Patrick is not found under Flynn.

S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is in the project tree but has no assertions or relationship citations for q_001. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); volume 007936749 likewise covers Schuylkill probate 1851-1930 browse-only (personCount 0) — this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 in Ireland) plausibly died between 1860 and 1900; this date window is set by Thomas's lifespan, not Patrick's. A will naming Patrick as a son, or letters of administration listing Patrick among the heirs, would be direct evidence of the father-son relationship. A will would also identify Thomas's wife — Patrick's mother — closing both parts of the parentage question. The loc_001 entry confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811.

The 1880 census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) was the first U.S. federal census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Patrick Flynn (~35 in 1880) may still be in Thomas Flynn's household with his relationship stated as 'son,' which would be stronger corroboration than the 1850 co-enumeration (a_004) that infers parentage only from household position. Thomas Flynn (~62 in 1880) should also be searched as head. The relationship column makes this census year the highest-yield of the available census records for a parentage question. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census) is already in the project tree and cited in R1 (ParentChild relationship, quality 2), but no assertions have been extracted for q_001 — the proof summary confirms the 1860 census was not formally searched through the research pipeline. Collection 1473181 (name-searchable). Patrick (~15 in 1860) was likely still in Thomas's household; co-enumeration here fills the gap between the 1850 entry (a_004) and the 1880 entry (pli_003). The 1860 census does not state relationships, but consistent co-enumeration under the same head across multiple census years strengthens the household continuity argument. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

Patrick (~25 in 1870) may have established his own household by 1870. Thomas (~52) should still be alive. Collection 1438024 (name-searchable). Searching Thomas's 1870 household may reveal other children named alongside or instead of Patrick — their presence as Patrick's siblings would corroborate the parentage hypothesis through the FAN cluster. Even if Patrick is absent, documenting Thomas's continued presence in Schuylkill County through 1870 helps bound Thomas's death date and therefore the probate window in pli_002. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

Patrick Flynn (~55 in 1900) was still alive — he died in 1908 — and would appear in the 1900 census. Collection 1325221 (name-searchable). The 1900 census records each person's father's birthplace and mother's birthplace as separate columns, along with immigration year. These fields could corroborate Thomas Flynn's Irish origin and provide a first hint of the mother's origin, even if the mother is not yet named. Completing the census chain through 1900 also establishes Patrick's household composition eight years before his death. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

For a parentage question a dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other is required. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 in Ireland) likely married Patrick's mother before Patrick's birth ~1845. The date window is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan: born ~1818, he could have married from roughly 1835 to 1855. If Thomas married in Schuylkill County after immigrating, a Catholic church register would name both parties. The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection (name-searchable, personCount 982,415, 1708-1985) is the primary search. The mother's maiden name is the foundational fact for tracing the maternal line, and the marriage date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas's role as father. Note: if Thomas married in Ireland before emigrating, a search of Irish records would be required separately. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried. The loc_001 entry notes Catholic parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia through this period.

Pennsylvania civil registration did not begin until 1906, so church records are the primary source for pre-1906 vital events. This item searches the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection (name-searchable, personCount 982,415, 1708-1985) for baptisms and burials: a sibling's baptism naming both parents would directly corroborate Thomas as Patrick's father and identify the mother; Thomas Flynn's burial record would establish his death date, narrowing the probate window in pli_002. The loc_001 entry notes Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (and from 1868 the Diocese of Scranton covered northern counties, not Schuylkill). Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

Volume 007936751 (Church Records 1842-1895, browse-only, personCount 0) covers the same period as the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection but is unindexed. If Thomas Flynn's marriage (pli_007) is not found in the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search, browsing this volume image by image is the fallback. The loc_001 entry's quirk explicitly warns that some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups that require browsing image-by-image. This is an image browse, not a name search.

Volume 007936752 (Deed Records 1815-1900, 22% name-searchable) covers Schuylkill County land transactions. This is the required FAN item for a parentage question. Thomas Flynn's deeds name witnesses and adjoining landowners — his FAN cluster in the anthracite coal community. A deed with Patrick Flynn as co-grantor or grantee establishes a legal relationship between them that corroborates the parentage hypothesis. Boundary recitals naming Patrick Flynn as an adjoining owner would document geographic proximity consistent with the household sequence found in the census chain. The 78% of the volume that is not name-searchable may require browsing by date range once Thomas's approximate deed-transaction period is bounded by the census and probate searches above. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried in the searchable portion.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
